name: TypeScript
summary: JavaScript with a static, structural type system that is checked at build time and erased before the code runs; since version 7.0 its compiler is written in Go.
intro: TypeScript adds type annotations, interfaces and generics to JavaScript, and working JavaScript code is already TypeScript code. Types are structural: a value fits an interface if it has the right shape, whatever it was declared as, and most types are inferred from the values assigned. The compiler, `tsc`, checks the types and then emits plain JavaScript with them removed, so the program runs on any JavaScript engine and the types never change what it does at run time. By default it still emits code when there are type errors, which eases migrating old JavaScript; `noEmitOnError` stops that. Strictness is a dial: `strict` turns on checks such as `noImplicitAny` and `strictNullChecks`, and is the default since TypeScript 6.0.

Because the types are only erased, many tools run TypeScript without `tsc` and without checking it. Vite transpiles `.ts` files with the Oxc transformer and leaves type checking to the editor and the build. Node.js runs `.ts` files directly by default since v23.6 and v22.18, stable since v25.2 and v24.12: it replaces the type syntax with whitespace and refuses features that need real code generation, such as `enum` declarations, namespaces with runtime code and parameter properties. Deno runs TypeScript without configuration and type-checks only with `--check` or `deno check`. Type checking is therefore a separate step, typically `tsc --noEmit` in CI, and the `erasableSyntaxOnly` option keeps code within what these tools can strip.

TypeScript 6.0 (March 2026) was the last release built on the original JavaScript codebase and mostly prepared users for the next one. TypeScript 7.0 (July 2026) is a port of the compiler to Go, published as the same `typescript` npm package with the same `tsc` command. Microsoft measured full builds 8 to 12 times faster, partly by parsing, checking and emitting on several threads with shared memory. 7.0 has no programmatic API, so tools built on it, such as Vue, Svelte and Angular template checking, stay on 6.0 through the `@typescript/typescript6` package; the 7.1 beta of 20 October 2026 brings a new API.
strengths: Gradual adoption: rename a `.js` file, then turn up strictness option by option as the codebase allows
Structural types and inference describe how JavaScript is actually written, so most code needs few annotations
One checker drives the editor too: errors as you type, completions, go-to-definition and safe renames across a project
Since 7.0, a native, multithreaded compiler: the VS Code codebase builds in 10.6 seconds instead of 125.7
limits: Unsound by design and erased at run time: `any`, type assertions and data from the network can all disagree with the types, so input still needs runtime validation
Two toolchains in practice: fast tools strip types without checking them, so a separate `tsc` run is needed, and enums, namespaces and parameter properties don’t work in strip-only runtimes
TypeScript 7.0 ships without a programmatic API; linters and framework tools that depend on it stay on 6.0 until 7.1
Major versions change defaults: 6.0 turned on `strict`, defaulted `types` to an empty list deprecated ES5 output and `baseUrl`, and dropped AMD modules; 7.0 removes everything 6.0 deprecated

story: JavaScript was never designed for large applications, yet that is what web teams were building with it. On 1 October 2012 Microsoft released a preview of TypeScript, built by Anders Hejlsberg, lead architect of C#, with Steve Lucco and Luke Hoban. Any JavaScript could be pasted into it and still work; optional static types made larger programs easier to build; and the output was plain JavaScript that ran in any browser. The code was open source under Apache 2.0 from the first day.

TypeScript 1.0 shipped in April 2014, and the team began taking pull requests. That July it moved from CodePlex to GitHub with a new compiler about five times faster. TypeScript 2.0, in September 2016, gave `null` and `undefined` their own types under `--strictNullChecks`, so forgetting to handle a missing value became a compile error.

As codebases grew, the compiler itself, written in TypeScript, became slow to load and check very large projects. In March 2025 Hejlsberg announced a native port to Go, code-named Corsa, with the existing codebase called Strada. It shipped as TypeScript 7.0 in July 2026, after 6.0 removed old options to ease the move, and the Go code replaced the old code in the main repository.

choices.choice: A superset that compiles to clean JavaScript
choices.why: The design goals ask for no runtime overhead and clean, idiomatic, recognizable JavaScript output, so existing code, libraries and engines all keep working and the output is readable without TypeScript.
JavaScript code passes plain objects around and checks their properties, not their declared class. Typing by shape fits that, and erasable types mean no type information is needed at run time.

The design goals list a sound or “provably correct” type system as a non-goal, and aim for a balance between correctness and productivity, so common JavaScript patterns type-check without fighting the compiler.

choices.choice: Port the compiler to Go instead of rewriting it
choices.why: The new compiler had to behave like the old one. Idiomatic Go closely resembles the existing TypeScript code, so it could be ported rather than redesigned, and a garbage collector keeps the code simple while costing little in a compiler that mostly runs as a batch job.

timeline.text: Microsoft releases a TypeScript preview on 1 October, under Apache 2.0
TypeScript 1.0 in April; the project moves to GitHub in July
Anders Hejlsberg announces a native port of the compiler to Go in March
TypeScript 6.0 in March, the last JavaScript-based release; TypeScript 7.0, the Go port, in July
